unctuous

UNK-choo-us · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Unctuous means oily in manner -- charm, praise, or sympathy laid on so thick and so smoothly that it feels slippery and insincere.

The maître d's unctuous welcome, all bowing and compliments, made the diners suspicious of the bill to come.

Example

The car salesman's unctuous compliments about her taste made her trust him even less than his prices already had.

Flattery so heavy it makes someone trust you less, not more, is exactly unctuous.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

smarmy: Smarmy is the informal word for charm so slick it repels -- the grinning, self-satisfied manner of someone laying it on thick. Unctuous means nearly the same oily insincerity, but it is the formal, literary term, and it stretches beyond charm to fake solemnity and sympathy.

ingratiating: Ingratiating describes the purpose of the behavior: intentionally working to win someone's favor, usually through flattery and eager agreement. Unctuous describes the texture of the manner itself -- oily, overdone, insincere -- whether or not any favor is being chased.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

blunt: direct and plainspoken, without flattery

Where it sits · how fake the praise feels

flattering → unctuous → obsequious

flattering vs. unctuous: Flattering can be perfectly sincere and welcome, an ordinary compliment; unctuous adds an unpleasant sense that the flattery is fake and self-serving.

obsequious vs. unctuous: Obsequious (taught earlier in this course) describes an overall eager, please-at-all-costs manner toward someone in power, while unctuous is narrower, focused specifically on the oily, insincere quality of the flattery itself.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — unct: to anoint, smear with oil (Latin (unguere))

suffix — -uous: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together: Unctuous comes from Latin unguere ('to anoint, smear with oil') + -uous -- literally 'having an oily quality,' extended in a non-literal sense to oily, slick flattery.

Use the root in a new word: ointment: The same unguere root gives us the everyday word ointment, a soothing substance rubbed on the skin -- the same 'oily smoothness' image behind unctuous flattery.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Unctuous specifically names the oily, insincere quality of someone's flattery or manner, distinct from "obsequious" (taught earlier in this course), which describes a broader pattern of eager, please-at-all-costs behavior toward a superior.
